text:
**Short answer:** For a typical full-size fridge, aim for about 1,000 Wh to get through most of a day, or 1,400-2,000 Wh to cover a full 24 hours with margin. The inverter should have a surge rating of at least ~1,300 W.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Continuous output:** A full-size fridge runs at roughly 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers it ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Surge rating:** The compressor's startup spike is commonly 1,200-2,400 W. If the station's surge rating is lower, it can trip the moment the fridge kicks on ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Look for pure sine wave output too.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so daily use is far lower than the running watts suggest.
   - One guide estimates ~1,400 Wh per day and ~2,800 Wh for two days, including inverter losses and 20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
   - Another estimates a ~1,000 Wh unit lasts about 17 hours ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
   - Estimates vary by source, so treat these as a range, not a promise.

## Get your own number
Find the yellow EnergyGuide label on your fridge. Take kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 for average watts, then multiply by 24 hours, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, and add ~20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Large side-by-sides with ice makers can use about double an efficient top-freezer, and frequent door opening raises it too. Keeping the door shut helps a lot.

## Options that fit
Prices below are from Dealectric, last tested Oct 21-24, 2026, and may change. These are affiliate links, so Dealectric is paid if you buy, at no cost to you.

| Outage length | Station | Specs | Price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short outages (about half a day to most of a day) | [BLUETTI AC180](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180) | 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W surge | $499 ($474.05 with code AFF5OFF) |
| Budget | [ALLPOWERS P1800](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-p1800-1024wh) | 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W, 3,600 W peak | $439 ($395.10 with code ALLPOWERS26) |
| A day or two | [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) | 2,073.6 Wh, 2,600 W, 3,900 W surge | $899 ($854.05 with AFF5OFF) |
| Expandable later | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) | 2,048 Wh, expandable to 8,192 Wh | $899 ($854.05 with AFF5OFF) |
| Multi-day | [BLUETTI Elite 300](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-300) | 3,014 Wh, 2,400 W, 4,800 W surge | $1,199 (pre-order, shipping from Oct 23) |

The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) is another 2 kWh-class option, listed at $699.99 after coupon on Anker's page.

Skip stations under ~500 Wh, such as the Tenergy T320, BLUETTI Elite 30 V2, and ALLPOWERS R600. They're meant for phones, laptops, and CPAP machines, not a fridge.

## My suggestion
If your area has outages of a few hours, the AC180 is enough. If you want a full day or more with a buffer for lights and a router, the Elite 200 V2 is the better fit. If you tell me your fridge's EnergyGuide kWh/year and how long your outages typically last, I can narrow it down.
